questions.stem: Why do biologists call mutation the ultimate source of genetic variation?
options: It is the only process that changes allele frequencies
It always produces alleles that improve survival
It is the process that sorts alleles into gametes
It is the only process that creates new alleles
questions.explanation: Only mutation produces alleles that did not exist before. Natural selection, gene flow and drift change the frequencies of existing alleles, and most mutations are neutral or harmful rather than helpful.

questions.stem: Which description defines the gene pool of a population?
options: All the chromosomes found in a single gamete
All the alleles of all the genes in a population
All the genes carried by one individual organism
All the species living together in one ecosystem
questions.explanation: The gene pool is the total set of alleles in an interbreeding population. Evolution is a change in the allele frequencies of a gene pool over generations.

questions.stem: In a population of 200 frogs, 72 are BB, 96 are Bb and 32 are bb. What is the frequency of allele b?
questions.explanation: There are 400 alleles in total. Allele b is carried twice by each bb frog and once by each Bb frog: (2 × 32) + 96 = 160, and 160/400 = 0.4. The figure 0.16 is the proportion of bb frogs, not the frequency of b.

questions.stem: Which mutation can be passed on to the next generation in an animal?
options: A mutation in a skin cell caused by ultraviolet light
A mutation in a liver cell caused by a toxic chemical
A mutation in a muscle cell during growth and repair
A mutation in a cell that will produce eggs or sperm
questions.explanation: Only mutations in the germline, the cells that give rise to gametes, can enter the next generation and the gene pool. Mutations in body cells are lost when the individual dies.

questions.stem: A mutation changes one base in a gene, but the protein produced is unchanged, and so is the phenotype. How will natural selection act on this new allele?
options: It will increase the allele's frequency, because new alleles are favoured
It will act on it only in individuals who are homozygous for it
It cannot act directly on it, because selection acts on phenotypes
It will remove the allele quickly, because all mutations are harmful
questions.explanation: Natural selection acts on differences in phenotype that affect survival and reproduction. An allele with no effect on phenotype is neutral, so its frequency can change only by chance, through drift. Many mutations are neutral, not harmful.

questions.stem: In evolution, what is meant by a selection pressure?
options: The movement of alleles into a population when individuals migrate into it
The chance loss of alleles from a population that has very few individuals
A factor in the environment that affects which individuals survive and reproduce
A change in the DNA of a gamete that produces a brand new allele in a population
questions.explanation: Selection pressures, such as predators, disease, climate or food supply, cause individuals with some phenotypes to survive and reproduce more than others. A change in DNA is a mutation, and migration of alleles is gene flow.

questions.stem: Which sequence best describes evolution by natural selection?
options: A selection pressure acts; individuals mutate as needed; they pass on the new alleles; the population soon adapts
Individuals try to adapt; they acquire useful traits in their lifetime; they pass these on to offspring
A population becomes isolated; all individuals change in the same way; a new species forms quickly
Variation exists; a selection pressure favours some phenotypes; they reproduce more; allele frequencies change
questions.explanation: Selection needs existing heritable variation. Individuals with favourable phenotypes survive and reproduce more, so their alleles become more common over generations. Mutations are random and do not arise because they are needed.

questions.stem: When an antibiotic is used, a population of bacteria quickly becomes mostly resistant to it. What best explains this?
options: The antibiotic made the bacteria's immune system stronger
Resistant bacteria already present survived and reproduced while others died
The antibiotic caused the bacteria to mutate into resistant forms
The bacteria learned to break down the antibiotic after exposure
questions.explanation: Resistance alleles arose by random mutation before the antibiotic was used. The antibiotic is a selection pressure that kills susceptible bacteria, leaving resistant ones to multiply. It does not cause the mutations that make bacteria resistant.

questions.stem: Myxoma virus was released in Australia to control rabbits and at first killed most infected rabbits. Over the following decades, the proportion of rabbits that survived infection increased. Which is the best explanation?
options: Rabbits with heritable resistance survived and passed on their alleles
Surviving rabbits made antibodies that they passed on in their genes
The virus made rabbits mutate in ways that protected them from it
Rabbits learned to avoid the virus and then taught this to their young
questions.explanation: Some rabbits carried alleles giving resistance. They were more likely to survive and breed, so resistance alleles increased in frequency. Antibodies made in a lifetime are not inherited through genes.

questions.stem: On a Galapagos island, a drought killed most plants with small soft seeds, leaving mainly large hard seeds. The next generation of finches had deeper beaks on average. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Each bird's beak grew deeper during the drought as it cracked larger seeds
The drought caused mutations that made beaks deeper in the next generation
Birds with shallow beaks chose to leave the island and live somewhere else
Birds with deeper beaks survived better and passed on heritable beak depth
questions.explanation: Finches with deeper beaks could crack the remaining hard seeds, so they survived and bred more. Because beak depth is heritable, the average in their offspring increased. A change acquired during one bird's life is not inherited.

questions.stem: Cane toads at the front of their spread across northern Australia have longer legs on average than toads in long-established areas. Which explanation best accounts for this?
options: Toads with longer legs spread faster, so they reach the front and breed with each other there
Each toad's legs lengthen through use as it travels longer distances to new areas
Longer legs arose by mutation only after the toads reached the hotter northern areas
Toads in established areas lose their long legs because they no longer need them
questions.explanation: Toads that travel faster, helped by longer legs, end up at the front and breed with other fast toads, so heritable long-leg alleles become concentrated there. Changes acquired through use are not inherited.

questions.stem: Which statement about natural selection is correct?
options: It always leads to organisms that are perfectly suited to their environment
It acts on individuals, changing their genotypes during their lifetime
It can only act on variation that is already present in a population
It produces the new alleles that a population needs to survive
questions.explanation: Selection sorts existing heritable variation; it cannot create the variation it needs. Individuals do not evolve during their lifetime; populations evolve as allele frequencies change across generations.

questions.stem: What does it mean for a trait to give a selective advantage?
options: It is acquired during life and helps that individual to live for a much longer time
It is dominant, so it is always expressed in every individual that carries it
It is new, so it has just been produced by a mutation in the population
It is heritable and increases an individual's chance of surviving and reproducing
questions.explanation: A selective advantage is a heritable phenotype that helps its carriers survive and leave more offspring in a particular environment, so its alleles increase in frequency. Dominant alleles are not necessarily advantageous.

questions.stem: Mice living on dark volcanic rock are mostly dark-furred, while mice of the same species on nearby pale sand are mostly pale. Owls hunt both by sight. What is the main selection pressure on fur colour?
options: The colour of the ground, which changes the fur colour of each mouse directly
Competition between the dark and pale mice for the same burrows and food
Mutation, which produces dark fur on rock and pale fur on sand as required
Predation by owls, which find mice that contrast with the ground more easily
questions.explanation: Owls catch mice that stand out against the background more often, so on each surface the camouflaged colour survives and breeds more. The ground does not change a mouse's fur, and mutations are not produced as required.

questions.stem: Which process consistently changes allele frequencies in a way that makes a population better suited to its environment?
options: The founder effect
A population bottleneck
Natural selection
Genetic drift
questions.explanation: Only natural selection favours alleles because of their effect on survival and reproduction, so it is the process that produces adaptation. Drift, founder effects and bottlenecks change frequencies by chance, which can even make a population less well suited.

questions.stem: What is gene flow?
options: The production of new alleles when DNA is copied incorrectly
The transfer of alleles from parents to offspring in gametes
The movement of alleles between populations through migration and interbreeding
The random change in allele frequencies from one generation to the next
questions.explanation: Gene flow happens when individuals or their gametes move between populations and breed, carrying alleles with them. Random change in allele frequency is genetic drift.

questions.stem: Two populations of the same species of possum live in forests joined by a strip of bushland. What is the effect of possums moving along the strip and breeding?
options: It makes the two populations become separate species
It causes new mutations to appear in both populations
It greatly increases genetic drift in both of the populations
It keeps the gene pools of the two populations similar
questions.explanation: Gene flow shares alleles between the populations, which counters the differences that selection and drift would otherwise build up. Speciation needs gene flow to stop, not continue.

questions.stem: What is genetic drift?
options: A change in allele frequencies due to new mutations
A change in allele frequencies due to chance events
A change in allele frequencies due to migration
A change in allele frequencies due to selection
questions.explanation: Genetic drift is random change in allele frequencies, because chance decides which individuals happen to survive and breed. It is not driven by how well suited an allele is to the environment.

questions.stem: Why does genetic drift have a much greater effect in small populations than in large ones?
options: Gene flow into small populations brings in many more alleles than into large populations
Chance events can change allele frequencies by a large amount when few individuals breed
Mutations happen more often in small populations because they are under more stress
Selection pressures are stronger in small populations, so alleles change faster
questions.explanation: In a small population the random survival or death of a few individuals is a large share of the gene pool, so allele frequencies can swing widely and alleles can be lost. In large populations chance effects tend to average out.

questions.stem: A storm randomly kills half the beetles on a small island, regardless of their colour. Afterwards, the frequency of the green allele has fallen from 0.5 to 0.3. Which process explains this change?
options: Mutation, because the storm damaged the beetles' DNA
Genetic drift, because the deaths were random with respect to colour
Natural selection, because the green beetles were less suited to the storm
Gene flow, because the storm carried beetles to other islands
questions.explanation: The storm killed beetles regardless of phenotype, so the change in allele frequency happened by chance: genetic drift. Natural selection would require colour to affect which beetles survived.

questions.stem: A few birds blown to a remote island start a new population. By chance, an allele that is rare on the mainland is common among them. What is this an example of?
options: Gene flow between the island and the mainland
Natural selection for the rare allele
The founder effect, a form of genetic drift
A population bottleneck caused by disease
questions.explanation: When a small group founds a new population, its allele frequencies can differ from the source population by chance. This founder effect is a form of drift. A bottleneck is a sharp fall in an existing population's size.

questions.stem: Which description fits a population bottleneck?
options: A barrier that splits one population into two separate populations
A movement of many individuals from one population into another
A sharp reduction in population size that leaves a small, less diverse gene pool
A gradual increase in population size as more food becomes available
questions.explanation: A bottleneck happens when an event such as hunting, disease or habitat loss kills most of a population. The survivors carry only part of the original genetic diversity. A barrier splitting a population is geographic isolation.

questions.stem: Why does a population that has passed through a bottleneck have an increased risk of extinction, even after its numbers recover?
options: Mutations stop occurring in small populations, so no new alleles can ever arise
Low genetic diversity means fewer individuals may have alleles to survive a new disease or change
The population grows so fast after the bottleneck that it uses up all of its food supply
The surviving individuals cannot reproduce sexually, so they produce only clones
questions.explanation: Recovered numbers do not restore lost alleles. With less variation, there is less chance that some individuals can survive a new pathogen or environmental change. Mutation continues but replaces lost diversity very slowly.

questions.stem: Northern elephant seals were hunted until very few remained. Their numbers have since recovered greatly, but they show very little genetic variation. Which explanation is best supported?
options: Gene flow from southern elephant seals has replaced the lost northern alleles
The bottleneck removed many alleles, and recovery came from the few survivors
Hunting caused mutations that removed variation from the survivors' gametes
Natural selection after recovery favoured seals with identical genotypes
questions.explanation: The present population descends from a small number of survivors, so it carries only the alleles they happened to have. Population growth increases numbers but not diversity. Hunting does not cause mutations.

questions.stem: A conservation program for a small, isolated population of an endangered marsupial moves a few animals in from a separate population. What is the main genetic aim?
options: To cause mutations in the gametes of the small population's animals
To introduce new alleles by gene flow, increasing genetic diversity
To produce a new species by joining two different gene pools
To increase genetic drift so that harmful alleles are lost faster
questions.explanation: Moving animals between populations creates gene flow, adding alleles that the small population has lost and reducing the risks of low diversity. Increasing drift would further reduce diversity.

questions.stem: Which definition of a species is used when studying speciation in sexually reproducing organisms?
options: Organisms that look alike and live in the same habitat
Organisms that have exactly the same alleles for every gene
Organisms that share a common ancestor at any time in the past
Organisms that can interbreed in nature and produce fertile offspring
questions.explanation: Under the biological species concept, a species is a group that can interbreed naturally to produce fertile offspring. Members of a species do not share identical alleles, and appearance alone can mislead.

questions.stem: Which sequence of events leads to speciation in geographically isolated populations?
options: Barrier forms; gene flow stops; populations change under different pressures; reproductive isolation develops
Populations change under different pressures; a barrier forms; gene flow increases; the populations merge
Gene flow increases; a barrier forms; populations become identical; reproductive isolation then develops
Reproductive isolation develops; a barrier forms; gene flow increases; the populations soon become genetically identical
questions.explanation: A barrier stops gene flow. Each population then changes through different selection pressures, mutation and drift, until they can no longer interbreed even if they meet again.

questions.stem: Rising sea levels separate an island population of lizards from the mainland population. Which factor would most speed up their divergence?
options: Very different selection pressures on the island and the mainland
Regular migration of lizards between the island and the mainland
Identical climate, predators and food on the island and the mainland
A very large population size on both the island and the mainland
questions.explanation: Different selection pressures favour different phenotypes in each population, so their gene pools diverge faster. Migration means gene flow, which keeps the gene pools similar, and large populations reduce the effect of drift.

questions.stem: Two populations of a fish were separated by a waterfall for thousands of years. When brought together in a tank, they mate but their hybrid offspring are all infertile. What does this show?
options: They are still one species, because they share a fairly recent common ancestor
They have become separate species, because they cannot produce fertile offspring
They are still one species, because they are able to mate and produce offspring
They have become separate species, because they now look different from each other
questions.explanation: Producing only infertile hybrids means the populations are reproductively isolated, so under the biological species concept they are separate species. Being able to mate is not enough; the offspring must be fertile.

questions.stem: Two populations of snails were isolated on either side of a mountain range. Population A lives in a dry area with bird predators, and population B in a wet area with crabs that crush shells. After many generations they cannot interbreed. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: The snails on each side mutated in the same ways because they needed to become separate species
Gene flow across the mountains carried different alleles to each side, producing two new species
Genetic drift alone made the populations identical, so they no longer recognised each other as mates
Isolation plus different selection pressures led their gene pools to diverge until they became reproductively isolated
questions.explanation: The mountain range stopped gene flow, and different predators favoured different shell and behaviour traits. Over time the gene pools diverged until the populations were reproductively isolated. Mutations are random and do not occur because they are needed.

questions.stem: What is micro-evolution?
options: Changes in an individual's phenotype during its own lifetime
Small changes in allele frequencies within a population over generations
The formation of new species and larger groups over long periods
The evolution of microscopic organisms such as bacteria and protists
questions.explanation: Micro-evolution is change in allele frequencies within a population, such as the rise of antibiotic resistance. Macro-evolution is the larger-scale change that produces new species and groups.

questions.stem: Which statement links micro-evolution to macro-evolution correctly?
options: They are driven by completely different processes that never interact
Micro-evolution happens only in animals, and macro-evolution only in plants
Micro-evolutionary changes accumulate over long periods to produce speciation
Macro-evolution happens first, and then it produces micro-evolutionary changes
questions.explanation: The same processes, natural selection, mutation, gene flow and drift, drive both. Many small changes in allele frequency, accumulated in isolated populations, eventually produce new species and larger groups.

questions.stem: Which example is macro-evolution rather than micro-evolution?
options: A rise in the frequency of dark moths in a population near a polluted city
The divergence of one ancestral species into several separate species
An increase in the frequency of insecticide resistance in a fly population
A change in the average beak depth of a finch population after a drought
questions.explanation: The formation of new species is macro-evolution. The other examples are shifts in allele frequency within one population, which are micro-evolution.

questions.stem: Which statement about the history of life on Earth is supported by evidence?
options: The number of species on Earth has stayed about constant since life first began
Life has changed and diversified over time, with simpler forms appearing first
All species alive today appeared at the same time and have not changed
Complex animals appeared first and later gave rise to single-celled organisms
questions.explanation: The fossil record and molecular evidence show that life began as simple single-celled forms and diversified over billions of years, with extinctions along the way. Species have not stayed constant in number or form.

questions.stem: A population of insects is split by a new highway. Which observation would be the earliest sign of micro-evolution in one of the populations?
options: The two populations being unable to produce fertile hybrid offspring
The appearance of a completely new body plan in one population
Fossils of the insects being found in rocks near the highway
A measurable change in an allele's frequency between generations
questions.explanation: Micro-evolution is detected as a change in allele frequencies over generations, which can happen quickly. Reproductive isolation marks speciation, which takes much longer.

questions.stem: Which combination of conditions makes evolution of a population by genetic drift least likely?
options: A population that has just been reduced to only a few dozen survivors
A very large population with gene flow from neighbouring populations
A very small population that is isolated from all other populations
A small population formed by a few founders on a remote island
questions.explanation: Drift is weakest in large populations, where chance effects average out, and gene flow replaces alleles lost by chance. Small, isolated, founder and bottlenecked populations are all strongly affected by drift.

questions.stem: A gene has two alleles in a lizard population. Over 20 generations the frequency of one allele rises from 0.2 to 0.7 in a large population, and the allele makes lizards harder for birds to see. Which process most likely caused the change?
options: Gene flow, because the allele makes lizards more likely to migrate to new areas
Mutation, because the allele appeared again and again in each new generation
Natural selection, because the allele improves survival in the presence of predators
Genetic drift, because large populations show strong random changes in allele frequency
questions.explanation: A steady rise in a large population, where drift is weak, linked to an allele that improves survival against predators points to natural selection. Repeated mutation is far too rare to cause such a large change.
